why_angle: The Paperless-ngx docs, setup guides and NAS roundups the shopper sees give no wattage or running cost for any NAS. rackdiff.com even leaves the power line of its cost table blank. This page turns each maker's own power figure into kWh and dollars a year at the EIA August 2026 US rate (18.16¢/kWh). It covers every candidate, and the result is about $26 a year for the DXP2800 against $46 to $67 for the TS-264, DS925+ and DXP4800 Plus.
must: 16.38 W with drives active, about $26 a year

page.h1: Best NAS for running Paperless-ngx as a scanned document archive (2026)
page.desc: Which NAS runs Paperless-ngx in Docker with PostgreSQL on an SSD and OCR, and what each one costs to keep running 24/7. Each maker's wattage is turned into kWh and dollars a year, with Synology's M.2 SSD rule.
page.answer: Short answer. The best NAS for running Paperless-ngx as a scanned document archive is the UGREEN NASync DXP2800: Intel N100 and 8 GB RAM for Docker and OCR, two NVMe slots for Postgres storage, and 16.38 W with drives active, about $26 a year of power around the clock.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Each yearly figure is the maker's own wattage × 8,760 hours × 18.16¢/kWh. That is the US average residential electricity price for August 2026 (EIA).

  • UGREEN DXP2800: 16.38 W × 8.76 = 143.5 kWh × $0.1816 = $26.06 a year with drives active; 5.24 W with drives asleep = $8.34.
  • Synology DS225+: 16.98 W → 148.7 kWh → $27.01; asleep 6.08 W → $9.67.
  • Synology DS725+ (not in the table): 20.41 W → 178.8 kWh → $32.47; asleep 7.87 W → $12.52.
  • Asustor AS5402T: 22.9 W → 200.6 kWh → $36.43; asleep 12.7 W → $20.20.
  • QNAP TS-264-8G: 29.086 W → 254.8 kWh → $46.27; asleep 18.288 W → $29.09.
  • Synology DS925+: 37.91 W → 332.1 kWh → $60.31; asleep 12.33 W → $19.61.
  • UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: 42.36 W → 371.1 kWh → $67.39; asleep 18.12 W → $28.83.
  • Five years, DXP2800 against TS-264: (46.27 − 26.06) × 5 = $101.05 saved.
  • Five-year cost to own at UGREEN's store price plus drives-active power: DXP2800 389.99 + 5 × 26.06 = $520.29; DXP4800 Plus 619.99 + 5 × 67.39 = $956.94.
Your archiveFits
Paperless-ngx only, a few dozen scans a week, Postgres on NVMe, two mirrored HDDsUGREEN DXP2800 {buy:ugreen-nasync-dxp2800}. Its warranty is 2 years (The Gadgeteer), against 3 years for the Synology, QNAP and Asustor units.
You want Synology DSM and a small archive, with Postgres on the HDD mirrorSynology DS225+, or the DS725+ if you will buy a Synology-verified M.2 SSD
Many SSDs and a ready-made Paperless-ngx packageAsustor AS5402T (4 M.2 slots; the Paperless-ngx package in Asustor's App Central uses MariaDB rather than PostgreSQL)
Paperless-ngx plus many other Docker apps, four baysUGREEN DXP4800 Plus {buy:ugreen-nasync-dxp4800-plus} (RAM up to 64 GB, KitGuru), or the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro, which ships with 32 GB DDR5 and an 8-core Intel Core i3 for $759.99 (TerraMaster, 2026-11-13)

What a Paperless-ngx NAS costs to run, year after year

A document archive sits idle almost all day. Paperless-ngx runs OCR only when a scan lands in the consume folder, so the box's resting draw sets the electricity bill, not its peak. Over a 5 to 10 year archive, that resting draw can add up to a sizeable share of what you paid for the NAS.

The makers test differently, so treat cross-brand gaps as rough. UGREEN's lab used Seagate 2 TB drives. QNAP tests with every bay filled, which is the harder test. Synology and Asustor publish an access figure and a hibernation figure from their spec sheets. Each model's own figure is solid; the gaps between brands are approximate.

Measured at the wall by named reviewers:

  • igor'sLAB: DXP2800 at 5.6 W in standby and 14.5 W during data transfer, with one NVMe SSD and no hard drives fitted (5.6 W × 8.76 ≈ 49 kWh a year before HDDs).
  • Dong Knows Tech: DS225+ at about 275 Wh per 24 hours with two Synology 4 TB HDDs (275 ÷ 24 ≈ 11.5 W average, ≈ 100 kWh a year).
  • KitGuru: DXP4800 Plus at 24.25 W idle on 2.5GbE and 30.45 W on 10GbE, with WD Red 6 TB drives (24.25 × 8.76 ≈ 212 kWh a year).

Letting the drives sleep is where the savings are. The asleep figures above are about a third to two thirds of the active ones. Hard drives can only spin down when nothing writes to them. Putting PostgreSQL and the app data on an SSD leaves the HDD mirror holding just the originals and archived PDFs. On the DXP2800 the two M.2 slots take NVMe for cache or extra storage (The Gadgeteer). On the Synology DS725+ and DS925+, Synology's spec pages say creating an M.2 storage pool requires Synology-verified SSDs, so budget for one.

Not recommended

Synology DS225+ for the SSD-plus-mirror layout. Synology's spec page lists 2 GB of RAM installed, a 6 GB maximum, and no M.2 slot. An SSD for the database would take one of its two bays, which leaves your scanned originals with no RAID 1 mirror. It is cheap to run, at $27.01 a year with drives active. It works if you keep Postgres on the mirrored HDDs, but for the layout above, the DXP2800 does the job and draws less power with drives active.
